title: PhD Salary After Tax: What Doctoral Students Actually Take Home in Europe

intro: Gross PhD salaries mislead — net pay decides your life. What doctoral researchers actually take home across eight European systems.
description: PhD salaries after tax across Europe: net monthly pay in Switzerland, Norway, Netherlands, Sweden, Finland, Denmark, Germany and the UK.
author: NextApply Team
excerpt: What PhD salaries pay after tax across eight European systems — the net numbers that decide your standard of living.
content:
Every PhD salary table on the internet compares gross numbers, and every gross comparison is misleading in the same way: European tax and social-security systems differ so much that a "higher" salary can leave less money in your account. What actually decides your standard of living for four years is the net figure — what lands in the bank each month — measured against the rent where you land. This guide does that arithmetic for the eight systems doctoral applicants compare most often.

The net comparison

Figures below use 2026 salary levels, standard single-person tax treatment, and approximate euro conversions; individual circumstances — church tax in Germany, municipal rates, pension choices — move each number by a few per cent. Treat the table as calibration, not payroll.

[[chart:phd-net-pay]]
CountryTypical grossApprox. net/monthNote
SwitzerlandCHF 50,000-62,000/yr€3,900-4,900Highest net in Europe; high costs offset
NorwayNOK 550,000-575,000/yr€3,200-3,400Excellent benefits; high living costs
Netherlands€2,900-3,700/month€2,250-2,850No tuition; housing is the squeeze
SwedenSEK 34,500/month avg€2,300-2,450Salary rises yearly; strong job security
Finland€2,600-3,900/month€2,050-2,900Rises with thesis progress
DenmarkDKK 28,900-35,000/month€2,050-2,450Highest costs of the Nordics
Germany€4,500-5,300/month (65% E13)€1,750-2,100Cheapest big-city living of the group
UK (stipend)£21,805/yr tax-free€2,100 equivalentNo tax or NI; London weighting +£2,000

Three structural findings matter more than any single row. First, Switzerland is in its own league: net pay runs nearly double the European average, which is why even Zurich’s rents leave doctoral researchers better off than anywhere else. Second, the UK stipend is tax-free by design — £21,805 with no income tax or national insurance nets higher than German gross salaries twice the size, though London rents erase the advantage fast (our UKRI stipend guide has the full picture). Third, the Nordics trade net pay for security — pension contributions, parental leave and unemployment insurance are inside those tax rates, and the same contributions continue towards permanent residence.

Gross versus net: why the rankings shuffle

Germany illustrates the shuffle perfectly. Its gross doctoral pay (€4,500-5,300 at 65 per cent TV-L E13) looks mid-table — until you notice the Netherlands nets more from a nominally lower gross, because Dutch payroll taxes start lower and German social contributions eat 20 per cent. Norway flips the other way: huge gross, hefty tax, still the second-best net on the list. And Denmark’s headline DKK figure, converted and taxed, lands below Finland’s net — a fact no gross comparison would ever reveal. Our gross comparison guide pairs with this one: gross for savings potential, net for daily life.

Stipends versus salaries — the tax difference that reshapes the table

The table’s strangest row is the UK’s, and the reason is structural: UKRI stipends are not salaries, so no income tax and no national insurance touch them — £21,805 gross is £21,805 net. Scholarship-funded places elsewhere work the same way: Dutch and German scholarship stipends are often (not always) tax-privileged, which is why a €1,500 monthly scholarship can outspend a €2,100 salary after deductions. Employment-model countries — Germany, the Netherlands, the Nordics, Switzerland — pay salaries precisely because the tax treatment buys pension credits, parental benefits and unemployment insurance: less cash today, more security for the same years.

Top-ups blur the lines further. Swedish doctoral salaries step up annually; German 65 per cent contracts often grow to 75 or 100 per cent in later years; Swiss scales rise by age; and some universities add mobility or family supplements that never appear in the advertised range. When two offers look close on this table, ask both departments for the year-by-year net progression — the four-year sum, not the year-one rate, is the real comparison.

What net pay buys locally

  • Zurich: a room costs CHF 900-1,400 — painful, affordable on CHF 5,000+ net.
  • Stockholm: SEK 6,000-8,000 rooms against SEK 27,000 net — comfortable solo living.
  • Munich: €700-1,100 rooms on €1,900 net — the tightest big-city fit in Germany.
  • Oxford/London: £900-1,300 rooms against £1,817 net — workable outside London, tight in it.

Salary is also negotiable in exactly one direction: upwards through scholarships and top-ups. The live positions below — Swiss, Nordic, Dutch and German — all pay on the scales in this table, and several sit in the cities where the arithmetic works hardest.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which European country leaves PhD students with the highest net income?

On pure net numbers, Switzerland wins: CHF 53,500-73,100 gross converts to roughly CHF 3,700-5,000 net per month even after source tax. Norway follows at roughly NOK 33,000-35,000 net per month, then the Netherlands at about €2,200-2,500 net for a first-year CAO scale P contract, and Germany at roughly €2,100-2,250 net for a 65% E13 position.

Are stipends taxed the same as PhD salaries?

No, and the difference matters. Employment-based PhDs in the Netherlands, Germany, Scandinavia and Switzerland are taxed at source with full social coverage. Scholarship-based funding — DAAD grants, many French allocations and university stipends — is often tax-free or lightly taxed but excludes pension contributions and, in some countries, unemployment insurance. Compare total packages, not headline figures.

How much do PhD taxes actually cost per month?

As a single filer with no children, expect around 30-35% effective deductions in Denmark and Sweden, roughly 25-30% in Norway and the Netherlands, about 35-40% in Belgium and Germany (including social security), and under 10% source tax in Switzerland for low gross salaries. Germany's advantage is the annual tax return, which refunds several thousand euros for part-time doctoral researchers.
